introduction.heading: What Is Deployment & CI/CD?
introduction.description: Deployment is the step where your code stops being something that only runs on your machine and becomes something other people can actually open in a browser. For a long time that meant manually uploading files over FTP and hoping nothing broke. Modern hosting platforms - Vercel, Netlify, Render, and others - replace that with a git-based workflow: push to a repo, and the platform builds and publishes it for you. CI/CD is what happens before and around that push. Continuous Integration (CI) automatically runs your tests and checks on every change, so problems get caught in a pull request instead of in production. Continuous Deployment/Delivery (CD) is what ships a change once it passes - either automatically, or with one manual approval click. Together they turn "deploy" from a nerve-wracking manual event into something that happens safely, constantly, and mostly by itself.

concepts.title: Continuous Integration (CI)
concepts.description: Automatically building and testing every push and pull request, so bugs surface before a merge instead of after one

concepts.title: Continuous Deployment vs. Delivery
concepts.description: Continuous Delivery gets every passing change ready to ship but waits for a human to click "deploy"; Continuous Deployment skips that click and ships automatically once checks pass

concepts.title: Build-Time vs. Runtime
concepts.description: A frontend's build step bakes certain environment variables directly into the JS bundle it ships to browsers; a server reads its environment variables live, at runtime, and they never leave the server

concepts.title: Environment Variables & Secrets
concepts.description: Configuration and credentials a project reads from its environment instead of hard-coding, set in the hosting platform's dashboard and kept out of git entirely

concepts.title: Preview Deployments
concepts.description: Most modern hosts deploy every pull request/branch to its own temporary URL, so a reviewer can click around the actual running change before it ever reaches production

concepts.title: Rollback
concepts.description: Re-pointing production at a previous, already-built deployment when a new one breaks something - instant, since nothing has to rebuild

pipeline.heading: The Deployment Pipeline
pipeline.description: A single push sets off a chain of stages, and each one has to succeed before the next one starts. Whether that chain lives entirely inside a hosting platform, or is split across a separate CI tool and a hosting platform, the shape is the same: install, check, build, then - only if everything above passed - deploy.

gettingStarted.heading: Getting Started
steps: Push your project to a GitHub repository - these platforms deploy from a git repo, not a zip file you upload by hand
Sign up for Vercel, Netlify, or Render and "import" that repository - most frameworks are auto-detected, pre-filling the build command
Double check (or set) the build command (e.g. npm run build) and the output/publish directory (e.g. dist) if it wasn't detected correctly
Add any environment variables your app needs in the platform's dashboard - never commit a real .env file with secrets to git
Push to your default branch - the platform builds it automatically and hands you back a live URL
Open a pull request against that branch and confirm you get a separate preview URL for it before merging
Add a .github/workflows/ci.yml file so GitHub Actions runs lint/tests on every push and pull request, catching problems before they ever reach the hosting platform

fullExample.heading: Full Example, Step by Step
fullExample.title: A GitHub Actions workflow: test on every push, deploy on merge to main
fullExample.description: This is a complete, realistic CI/CD workflow file. It runs lint/test/build on every push and pull request targeting main, but only runs the deploy job - which needs a secret token - when the change has actually landed on main. Click through the steps to see which lines each one is talking about.

steps.label: Name the workflow
steps.explanation: This is just a display name - it's what shows up as the tab/label for this workflow in the GitHub Actions UI, and has no effect on when or how it runs.

steps.label: Choose the triggers
steps.explanation: on: lists the events that start this workflow. Listing both push and pull_request against main means every pull request gets tested before it's even mergeable, not just after someone merges it.

steps.label: Define the build-and-test job
steps.explanation: runs-on picks which virtual machine image the job executes on. Everything under steps: for this job runs, in order, on that one fresh VM.

steps.label: Check out the repository
steps.explanation: A GitHub Actions VM starts completely empty - actions/checkout is what actually clones your repo's code onto it before anything else can run.

steps.label: Set up the runtime
steps.explanation: actions/setup-node installs a specific, pinned Node version, so CI runs against the same version your project targets instead of whatever happens to be preinstalled.

steps.label: Install, lint, test, build
steps.explanation: npm ci installs exactly what's in package-lock.json (unlike npm install, it won't update anything), giving a reproducible install. Each following step has to exit successfully - a failing lint or test stops the job right there, and the deploy job below never even starts.

steps.label: Gate the deploy job
steps.explanation: needs: build-and-test makes this job wait for that one to fully pass. if: only lets it proceed on a push to main - so pull requests still get tested, but never trigger a deploy.

steps.label: Deploy using a secret
steps.explanation: This job runs on its own fresh VM too, so it checks out the code again, then runs the actual deploy command. The token itself is never written in the file - secrets.VERCEL_TOKEN pulls it from GitHub's encrypted repo secrets and injects it only as an environment variable for this one step.
